
## Uncertainty deductions

```{r}
#| label: or-uncertainty
#| output: false

readr::write_csv(uncertainty_table, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-uncertainty.csv")
fmt_tbl(uncertainty_table)
```

The published interval was wider than the reductions it qualified. Across the `r sum(!is.na(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]]))` crediting years with a positive mean reduction, the relative half width of the disaggregated account ran from `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent of the mean. The adjustment factor ran from `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent (Online Resource 8). In 2023 the mean reduction of `r round(mc_split$mean[mc_split$Year == 2023], 1)` Mt had a standard deviation of `r round(mc_split$sd[mc_split$Year == 2023], 1)` Mt and a 90 per cent interval of `r round(mc_split$q05[mc_split$Year == 2023])` to `r round(mc_split$q95[mc_split$Year == 2023])` Mt. On the threshold account the adjustment factor ran from `r min(uncertainty[["Threshold rule deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE)` to `r max(uncertainty[["Threshold rule deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE)` per cent, because its reductions were larger, not because its emissions were more certain.

The independent draws set the ceiling of that uncertainty. With half the error variance shared between the reference years and the crediting year, the interval of the disaggregated account ran from `r sh(0.5, "Interval, lowest (%)")` to `r format(sh(0.5, "Interval, highest (%)"), big.mark = ",")` per cent. Only `r sh(0.5, "Years keeping a credit")` of the `r sum(split_pos)` positive years kept a credit. With 90 per cent shared it ran from `r sh(0.9, "Interval, lowest (%)")` to `r format(sh(0.9, "Interval, highest (%)"), big.mark = ",")` per cent and `r sh(0.9, "Years keeping a credit")` years kept one. Every positive year kept a credit only when the shared share exceeded `r round(100 * rho_needed, 1)` per cent, which left each year's own error at `r round(100 * sqrt(1 - rho_needed), 1)` per cent of the published standard deviation. Because the two deductions were linear in the uncertainty, the point at which nothing was kept could be solved directly. It was `r round(100 * break_even())` per cent on the default buffer, `r round(100 * break_even("1,2,3"))` with all three mitigating factors and `r round(100 * break_even(after_reversal = TRUE))` after a reversal. Over the eight years the disaggregated account's total reduction was `r round(period_split[["total"]], 1)` Mt at `r round(100 * period_split[["ci"]])` per cent, a deduction of `r round(100 * trees_uncertainty(period_split[["ci"]]))` per cent, so the buffer left nothing. The threshold account totalled `r round(period_rule[["total"]], 1)` Mt at `r round(100 * period_rule[["ci"]])` per cent and kept `r round(100 * kept(period_rule[["ci"]]))` per cent, `r round(period_rule[["total"]] * kept(period_rule[["ci"]]), 1)` Mt.

## Fire estimates

Forest fires in Canada released `r format(round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / 1000), big.mark = ",")` Mt of carbon dioxide in 2023 on the FAOSTAT Tier 1 estimate, `r round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / mean(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year < 2023]), 1)` times the mean of the earlier years. The `r format(round(burn_2023$ha), big.mark = ",")` hectares of other forest it recorded as burned, at `r sprintf("%.1f", burn_2023$fuel)` tonnes of dry matter per hectare and `r format(table_2_5$co2[1], big.mark = ",")` g of carbon dioxide per kilogram, gave that total. Rerun from the note in Earth Engine, that burned area was reproduced within `r round(100 * max(abs(repro_year$ratio - 1)))` per cent in every year over the five items. Of the `r nrow(repro_item)` item and year values, `r round(repro_within_2)` per cent fell within 2 per cent of the published value. FAO classed 2023 with the 2022 land cover map and 2024 with the 2023 map, the latest it held. The forest pixels fell `r sprintf("%.2f", sum(forest_2023$ha[forest_2023$zone_group == 1]) / 1e6)` Mha in boreal and `r sprintf("%.2f", sum(forest_2023$ha[forest_2023$zone_group == 2]) / 1e6)` Mha in temperate zones. At the all boreal and all other temperate rows of Table 2.4 they gave `r sprintf("%.1f", fao_fuel_2023)` tonnes per hectare, the fuel FAO published. Across the `r nrow(gap)` years both sources reported, that estimate was a median of `r round(median(gap$Ratio), 1)` times the value Canada submitted. By Equations 3.1 and 3.2 the fuel term carried `r round(100 * u_fuel[1])` to `r round(100 * u_fuel[2])` per cent and the emission factor `r round(100 * u_ef)` per cent. Together they gave `r round(100 * u_forest[1])` to `r round(100 * u_forest[2])` per cent with no error in burned area, so the 2023 estimate lay within `r round(co2_2023 * (1 - u_forest[1]))` to `r round(co2_2023 * (1 + u_forest[1]))` Mt, an interval that contained zero. The coefficients recovered from the published values were the savanna and grassland factors of Table 2.5, `r coefficients[["CO2 (g/kg)"]][coefficients$Item == "Other forest"]` g of carbon dioxide and `r coefficients[["CH4 (g/kg)"]][coefficients$Item == "Other forest"]` g of methane per kilogram (Online Resource 4). The methane was `r round(100 * table_2_5$ch4[1] / table_2_5$ch4[2])` per cent of what the extra tropical forest row gave. The domain placed `r round(100 * sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]]) / sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]] + savanna_share[["Forest fires"]]))` per cent of the area burned over 2001 to 2024 in its savanna, grassland and shrubland items. Those burned at `r table_2_4$fuel[3]` and `r table_2_4$fuel[4]` tonnes per hectare with no carbon dioxide published.

```{r}
fmt_tbl(coefficients, right = c("Burned area (ha a year)", "Fuel (t/ha)", "CH4 (g/kg)", "N2O (g/kg)", "CO2 (g/kg)"))
```

Fuel burned and the emission factors are the zone's rows in Online Resource 2. The uncertainty is the Approach 1 half width of the 95 per cent interval for carbon dioxide, with no error on burned area. The last row is FAO's published value."

The national fire record placed `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(zone_2023$ha) / 1e6)` Mha of fire in Canada's ecological zones in 2023, `r round(boreal_share_2023)` per cent of it in the three boreal zones (@tbl-zones). Boreal tundra woodland alone burned `r sprintf("%.1f", zone_2023$ha[zone_2023$gez_abbrev == "Bb"] / 1e6)` Mha. At the boreal wildfire row of Table 2.4 and the extra tropical forest row of Table 2.5, Equation 2.27 gave `r format(round(sum(zone_2023$co2_mt)), big.mark = ",")` Mt of carbon dioxide for the year. That was `r round(sum(zone_2023$co2_mt) / co2_2023, 1)` times the `r round(co2_2023)` Mt FAO published from one coefficient, because FAO recorded `r sprintf("%.1f", burn_2023$ha / 1e6)` Mha of other forest burned against the `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(zone_2023$ha) / 1e6)` Mha of the national record. Methane came to `r format(round(sum(zone_2023$ch4_kt)), big.mark = ",")` kt against FAO's `r round(burn_2023$dm * burn_2023$ch4 / 1e6)` kt. The boreal row's standard error of 48.4 on a mean of 52.8 tonnes per hectare put the uncertainty of the national total at `r round(100 * u_2023)` per cent. The interval contained zero, as FAO's did.

```{r}
fmt_tbl(strata_table, right = names(strata_table)[-(1:2)])
```

Of the `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(strata_2023$ha) / 1e6)` Mha that burned in 2023, `r round(natural_share_2023)` per cent was recorded as natural in cause and `r round(human_share_2023)` per cent as human (@tbl-strata). Over 2001 to 2024 the natural share was `r round(natural_share_all)` per cent and no year fell below `r round(min(dplyr::summarise(dplyr::filter(cause_year, region == "Canada"), share = 100 * mha[cause == "Natural"] / sum(mha), .by = year)$share))` per cent (Online Resource 5). Agencies typed `r round(typed_share_2023)` per cent of the 2023 area as crown, surface or ground fire, so the general wildfire row carried the rest. Fires on organic soil covered `r round(organic_share_2023)` per cent of the area burned in Canada and `r round(bc_organic_share_2023)` per cent in British Columbia. The peat term added `r format(round(peat_2023), big.mark = ",")` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent to the `r format(round(veg_2023), big.mark = ",")` Mt of the vegetation term in Canada, and `r round(bc_peat_2023)` Mt to `r round(bc_veg_2023)` Mt in the province. FAO had computed Canada's organic soil fires at a mean of `r format(round(mean(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide a year over 2001 to 2021, and published zero. MCD12Q1 placed `r round(forest_share_2023)` per cent of the 2023 area in forest classes and `r round(savanna_share_2023)` per cent in woody savanna and savanna, which FAO burned at savanna fuel values. On the 2 km grid, `r sprintf("%.0f", fuel_area$mha[fuel_area$category == "Forest" & fuel_area$fuel == 52.8])` Mha of Canada drew the boreal forest row and `r sprintf("%.0f", fuel_area$mha[fuel_area$category == "Forest" & fuel_area$fuel == 19.8])` Mha the temperate row, with `r sprintf("%.0f", row_area$mha[row_area$row_class == "Boreal forest, organic soil"])` Mha of boreal forest on organic soil.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tier2
#| output: false

readr::write_csv(tier2_table, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-tier2.csv")
fmt_tbl(tier2_table)
```

The national layers divided the land that the defaults treated as one (Online Resource 7). Where Table 2.4 gave Canada's forest two rows, the fuel types gave conifer `r sprintf("%.0f", fbp_mha(fbp_labels[1]))` Mha, mixedwood `r sprintf("%.0f", fbp_mha(fbp_labels[2]))` Mha and deciduous `r sprintf("%.0f", fbp_mha(fbp_labels[3]))` Mha. The 2023 fires burned `r round(conifer_share_2023)` per cent of their area in conifer, `r round(mixed_share_2023)` per cent in mixedwood and `r round(deciduous_share_2023)` per cent in deciduous fuel (@fig-zones). The peatland map held `r sprintf("%.0f", cfs_peat_mha)` Mha of bog and fen against `r sprintf("%.0f", ipcc_organic_mha)` Mha of organic soil in the IPCC raster, and only `r sprintf("%.0f", both_peat_mha)` Mha was organic in both. The 2023 fires therefore fell `r round(cfs_peat_share_2023)` per cent on the peatland map against `r round(organic_share_2023)` per cent on the default raster. The National Burned Area Composite recorded `r sprintf("%.1f", nbac_2023 / 1e6)` Mha for 2023, between FAO's `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(used$ha[used$year == 2023]) / 1e6)` Mha across its items and the `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(strata_2023$ha) / 1e6)` Mha of the fire points. The inventory used none of the defaults, since it held a national dataset for every term [@eccc2026nir].

# Discussion

On the two lines of Canada's 2026 inventory, disaggregating natural disturbance decided whether an account existed to credit in 2017 to 2024. It did not make that account precise. The disaggregation was therefore the condition on which a credit existed, rather than an adjustment to a reported number. Earlier work found the same dependence, in that the division rather than the forest moved Canada's reported balance under Kyoto and after the harvest revision [@kurz2008risk; @kurz2024revised; @bysouth2024high]. A standard that took the reported balance as its input passed the division straight into the credit.

The disaggregated account kept part of its reductions in only `r sum(banked > 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(!is.na(banked))` years with a positive reduction, for an arithmetic rather than an ecological reason. An account whose emissions and removals nearly cancelled reported a relative half width far larger than either side of it, the case @paciornik2019uncertainties warned against interpreting. Canada's own inventory met it in 2024, when its Forest Land carbon dioxide was a net of −1.9 Mt within a 95 per cent interval of −63 to 19 Mt. Through Equations 10 and 11 the adjustment factor exceeded the reduction in `r sum(over, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(!is.na(over))` positive years. In `r mc_split$Year[which(banked > 0)]` the account kept `r round(banked[which(banked > 0)], 1)` per cent of its reduction, after the deduction and a buffer that the shortfall of `r min(credits$Year[!split_pos])` had raised to `r 100 * trees_buffer(after_reversal = TRUE)` per cent.

The length of the record mattered less to the classification than to the threshold. Canada applied no baseline at all but reconstructed the cause of every stand for 1889 to 1989 [@kurz2024revised]. Each burned area then stayed on the natural disturbance line for the 60 to 100 years it took to regrow to a harvestable age. Australia's inventory tested fire seasons against a 13 year mean [@bowman2023wildfire]. The European example in the guidance used the 20 years before the base year and assumed 20 years of regrowth [@ogle2019generic]. Three inventories thus used three record lengths under guidance that set none.

The balance the disaggregation rested on carried conditions that no crediting standard checked, and choices that moved the annual numbers a standard read. The 2019 Refinement set no time limit on the later removals and held that natural effects averaged out "provided that there are no trends in disturbance rates, such as increased annual area burned as a result of climate change" [@ogle2019generic, pp. 2.68 to 2.69]. The 2013 Supplement had made the same absence of trend the first condition for avoiding net credits [@ipcc2014kp, p. 2.50]. Methane and nitrous oxide were never balanced, because "non-CO2 emissions are not taken up by vegetation", yet the natural disturbance line was reported in carbon dioxide equivalent [@ogle2019generic, p. 2.72; @eccc2026nir]. The Refinement allowed natural emissions to be identified at "the individual (stand-level) disturbed areas or the total (landscape-level) emissions from all disturbances in the year" [@ogle2019generic, pp. 2.71 to 2.72]. It allowed later removals to be apportioned by the shares of area and stock lost, and held that the choices changed the annual split while "in the long term the totals are the same" [@ogle2019generic, pp. 2.71 to 2.72]. The 2013 Supplement had allowed no apportioning, since every excluded land was identified by "georeferenced location, year and types of disturbances" [@ipcc2014kp, p. 2.38]. It kept salvage logging in the account, where 2019 disaggregated it with removals split "proportionally to the C stock losses these activities have caused" [@ogle2019generic, p. 2.71]. A credit computed year by year therefore depended on choices the guidance said did not matter in the long run.

The rule that classed a year as natural also decided how much was credited, and the test behind the rule was met by statement. On Canada's inventory the threshold rule credited more than the disaggregated account. It kept the natural disturbance line in four of the five reference years and then left all of it out of the crediting years it classed as natural. It built the background level into the reference level, so that "emissions from natural disturbances up to the background level are already implicitly excluded", excluded only the emissions above that level, and urged "the longest available time series" [@ipcc2014kp, pp. 2.45 to 2.50]. Australia's inventory instead classed "all fire related GHG emissions (excluding prescribed fires) from that state or territory" as natural once a season passed both tests [@bowman2023wildfire]. Canada's natural disturbance line held every wildfire whatever its cause, under a definition that excluded fires "materially influenced by a country" [@eccc2026nir; @ogle2019generic, p. 2.69]. The 2013 Supplement asked for evidence of prevention and suppression effort [@ipcc2014kp, pp. 2.36 to 2.37]. The 2019 Refinement asked for the same evidence, and its European example answered that "All wildfires are considered not materially influenced" [@ogle2019generic, pp. 2.76 and 2.79]. The cause field of the national fire record placed `r round(natural_share_2023)` per cent of the 2023 area under natural ignition, and no inventory read here used it (@tbl-strata).

The fire emissions inside both accounts came from one method, whose fire matrices assumed high severity throughout [@thompson2026incorporating; @eccc2026nir]. The account without the disaggregation took nearly all of the 10 to 25 per cent a severity sub-model removed. FAO burned Canada's forest at the savanna and grassland emission factors, and propagated by Equations 3.1 and 3.2 its estimate was uncertain by `r round(100 * u_forest[1])` per cent or more. The check was therefore no more certain than the account it checked. Three things the note did not state had to be recovered before FAO's values could be rebuilt. They were the land cover year used for the latest years, the Table 2.4 row behind each item, and the savanna emission factor row applied to forest. Everything else the note stated was enough. Rebuilt by zone from the fire points, the same equation gave `r round(sum(zone_2023$co2_mt) / co2_2023, 1)` times FAO's value for 2023. Applied to FAO's own burned area, the zone rows gave `r format(round(rung2_2023$co2_mt), big.mark = ",")` Mt, `r sprintf("%.1f", rung2_2023$co2_mt / co2_2023)` times FAO's value, the part of that gap due to the rows alone. The remaining `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(zone_2023$co2_mt) / rung2_2023$co2_mt)` fold lay in the burned area. Neither estimate was more certain than its size, because the boreal wildfire row of Table 2.4 carried a standard error of 92 per cent of its mean [@aalde2006generic]. The peat term on organic soil added `r round(100 * peat_2023 / veg_2023)` per cent to the vegetation term, and the MCD12Q1 classes FAO burned at savanna fuel values held most of the area burned [@ipcc2014wetlands]. The stratum total of `r format(round(veg_2023 + peat_2023), big.mark = ",")` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent stood beside the 647 Tg of carbon that inverse modelling of satellite carbon monoxide gave for the same fires [@byrne2024carbon]. The national layers then divided every term the defaults had treated as one (Online Resource 7). The one boreal row became conifer, mixedwood and deciduous fuel, and the organic soil the third of the mapped peat on which the two layers agreed. The choice of layer therefore moved the estimate as far as the choice of tier, and Canada's inventory used none of the defaults [@eccc2026nir].

The silence a crediting standard inherited was deliberate. The 2019 Refinement placed its option within reporting, for countries that might otherwise act "outside the inventory process", and its boxes stated that each example "neither adds guidance nor overrules guidance" [@ogle2019generic, pp. 2.67 and 2.73]. The 2024 meeting held that "GHGI does estimation, not accounting" and that a disaggregated estimate "would be difficult to impossible" to verify with observations [@ipcc2024reconciling, pp. 59 and 16]. ART TREES cited the 2019 definition for its exclusion without saying how far back the record must reach [@art2025trees3]. Two countries applying the same clause to the same fire record could therefore report different natural shares. The accounting rule the IPCC had written for that exclusion sat in the 2013 Supplement [@ipcc2014kp, p. 2.45]. Five changes would close the gap. They were a stated record length, a stated regrowth period, an uncertainty deduction on gross emissions and removals, and buffers set from the regional fire regime [@marinelli2026risk; @wu2026global]. The fifth was to exclude only the emissions above a background level, as the Kyoto Protocol provision did. Two limits qualified these results. The uncertainty analysis applied one published interval to every annual value and treated each year's error as independent, which the shared share bounded without removing. All three accounts used Canada's figures as reported, so the study compared three sums of one model's output with FAOSTAT as its only independent estimate.

# Conclusions

Disaggregating natural disturbance decided whether Canada had a forest carbon credit to claim under ART TREES for 2017 to 2024, and it did not make that credit precise. With the disaggregation, Canada's managed land achieved `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent against the standard's crediting level. Without it the same land fell `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt short in 2023 alone. A country or province in a megafire regime could therefore report a creditable balance only by excluding the fires, under guidance that set no record length for doing so. The threshold rule, which excluded natural disturbance only in extreme fire years, gave `r round(sum(credits[["Threshold rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_pos]) / sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` times the disaggregated account because ordinary fire years raised its crediting level. The disaggregated account remained uncertain by more than its own size, with adjustment factors of `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent. Every positive year kept a credit only if more than `r round(100 * rho_needed, 1)` per cent of the error variance was shared between years, a share the inventory did not report. The Tier 1 fire estimate a government would check its inventory against rested on savanna factors its method did not state and was uncertain by `r round(100 * u_forest[1])` per cent or more. Its burned area was reproduced from the published method within `r round(100 * max(abs(repro_year$ratio - 1)))` per cent in every year once the land cover year, the Table 2.4 rows and the emission factor row it did not state were recovered. Rebuilt by stratum, it put `r round(natural_share_2023)` per cent of the 2023 area under natural ignition and `r round(organic_share_2023)` per cent on organic soil. The national layers of fuel, peat and burned area divided every term the defaults had treated as one. Standards that relied on the disaggregation needed a stated record length, a stated regrowth period and the exclusion of only the emissions above a background level. They also needed an uncertainty deduction on gross emissions and removals, and buffers set from regional fire regimes.
